name: Secrets Management Best Practices
description: This module captures the best practices for secrets management, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.
content:
This module captures the best practices for secrets management, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Re-check edge cases relevant to secrets management (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
2. When multiple secrets management strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
3. When secrets management decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
4. Surface known limitations of a chosen secrets management approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
5. Prefer the simplest secrets management approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
6. Measure before optimizing any secrets management bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
7. State assumptions about secrets management explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
8. Document any non-obvious secrets management decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
9. Before starting secrets management work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
10. Validate secrets management outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
11. Keep secrets management changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not apply generic secrets management advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid mixing unrelated secrets management concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not skip documenting secrets management assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for secrets management, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
